#19008. Industry News: Senate Passes Controversial Permitting Bill Aimed at Speeding Construction and Lowering Costs

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1216 w)
📖 Baca
Business & Policy ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Realtor ↗ Open Full Page

Industry News: Senate Passes Controversial Permitting Bill Aimed at Speeding Construction and Lowering Costs

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1216 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Realtor

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A bipartisan bill to streamline permitting for major infrastructure projects could have implications for both housing and energy costs.
  • Industry observers note that the Senate voted 62-33 to pass the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, or BAAJA, which would streamline permits and limit the scope of government reviews under the National Environmental Policy Act and Clean Water Act.
  • Senate committee leaders Sheldon Whitehouse (D-RI), Martin Heinrich (D-NM), Shelley Moore Capito (R-WV), and Mike Lee (R-UT) introduced the bill.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A bipartisan bill to streamline permitting for major infrastructure projects could have implications for both housing and energy costs.

Industry observers note that the Senate voted 62-33 to pass the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, or BAAJA, which would streamline permits and limit the scope of government reviews under the National Environmental Policy Act and Clean Water Act. Much of that was aimed at massive energy infrastructure, but it also has implications for housing and even data centers.

Senate committee leaders Sheldon Whitehouse (D-RI), Martin Heinrich (D-NM), Shelley Moore Capito (R-WV), and Mike Lee (R-UT) introduced the bill. It's since been attached to a larger and more popular bill, but lawmakers have been debating and tweaking it for several weeks.

The latest version released this month updated language to assuage concerns that it would weaken environmental protections and rights of Native American groups. The bill has been popular but divisive: While the speed would boost green energy like wind and solar power, plus electric infrastructure that lowers costs, it could also speed along fossil fuel investments, like natural gas pipelines, and nuclear power.

In a recent development, "Our permitting system takes too long, costs too much, and leaves too much uncertainty for the people trying to build what our country needs," Lee said on the floor before the vote. The bill could make "everything you buy" less expensive in the long run.

According to recent reports, but several housing advocates have cheered the bill, saying it would make it easier to build affordable housing and invest in local communities. They include the National Association of Home Builders, YIMBY Action, the Niskanen Center, Associated Builders and Contractors, and the National Community Development Association.

Sources indicate that "America’s housing shortage demands solutions that make it easier and more affordable to build," National Association of Realtors® Chief Advocacy Officer Shannon McGahn noted. NAR "supports streamlining permitting processes and reducing unnecessary regulatory burdens that drive up development costs, delay construction, and limit housing supply.".

A White House policy paper estimates federal permitting requirements for major infrastructure take 4.2 years to complete—and produce 1,700 pages of paperwork. It expects reforms to increase the GDP by $82 billion to $164 billion and produce $14 billion to $28 billion in tax revenue.

It also noted permitting reform could cut electric bills by $178 to $251 a year for the average household. President Donald Trump urged the bill's passage in a post on Truth Social, calling it "a BIG WIN.".

"This Landmark Permitting Reform Legislation will codify our America First Energy Agenda, and ensure that we can build Pipelines, Mines and Power Plants faster than ever before, lowering Energy Costs for American Families, and creating High Paying American Jobs," the president posted.

"We can lower costs, juice the clean energy economy, build major things again in America, reduce pollution, and create tons of new well-paying union jobs," Whitehouse stated.

A number of groups opposed to the bill argued that some of the protections it removes would endanger protections for Native American groups and hamstring environmental preservation.

The Association on American Indian Affairs said the bill would "threaten Native sovereignty and the protections that safeguard our country's cultural and historic heritage." The Endangered Species Coalition says it would weaken protections. Both continued to oppose the bill even as it was amended.

The House would need to vote on the bill next, and members have already began debating its merits.

Recent findings suggest that "Even as amended, it undermines Tribal sovereignty, environmental laws, and locks in dangerous projects," Rep. Melanie Stansbury (D-NM) stated in an X post. "This is NOT the deal, NOT the time, and NOT what the American people asked for.".

Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-SD) cast the bill as a way for Republicans to use the remaining weeks of their majority to improve affordability for Americans.

"One of the biggest things we can do to address affordability for the long term is to ensure a reliable and affordable energy supply," Thune said. “And that starts with ensuring that energy projects don’t face unnecessary permitting barriers.".

The federal permitting process, he later remarked, "has unfortunately gone far beyond these reasonable expectations.

“And that’s due in large part to senseless delays caused by cascading litigation from environmental groups and by agencies determined to study a project to death," Thune said. “We’ve seen those delays happen to everything from water projects to broadband deployment to affordable energy and improving roads and bridges.".

It has been revealed that A poll by moderate think tank Third Way found bipartisan support for the tenets of the bill. About 62% of respondents named lowering utility bills as a top concern, and 57% keeping the power grid reliable.

Industry observers note that “It’s more important than ever to pass permitting reform this year. The overwhelming support for the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act reflects the Senate’s commitment to addressing the nation's energy affordability challenges.".

According to recent reports, the bill was also host to Congress' latest effort to rein in data center developments proliferating throughout the country. One amendment by Sen. Ron Wyden (D-OR) would have banned data centers on public lands. Republicans blocked it.

"There is enormous concern that this bill puts the pedal to the floor on data centers across the country," Wyden stated on the floor.

It has been revealed that following Democrats' gains in the House after the 2026 midterms, a number of left-leaning groups have called for a hesitant Congress to formulate more laws involving data centers. Among them, the Chamber of Progress called for federal AI safety standards and requirements for data centers to cover their own costs.

It has been revealed that A recent study by the Wharton School indicates that data centers have indeed increased industrial electricity prices in the nation. But it also mentioned that residential customers absorbed relatively little of that price gain.

But that doesn't mean they don't affect communities. A group of Senate Democrats, including Elizabeth Warren of Massachusetts, Chris Van Hollen of Maryland, and Richard Blumenthal of Connecticut, released a report pinning other costs on them. It also criticized the tax incentives.

"This investigation finds the data center industry is bulldozing local communities and using their economic resources to play states and local communities against one another, creating a race to the bottom in which state and local policymakers feel they have no choice but to accede to the data centers’ demands—and leaving ordinary citizens stuck with the bills," they said in a joint statement.

Recent findings suggest that voter anger has put data center incentives in the spotlight. Virginia spent over $4 billion in data center incentives over 10 years, according to a state report. Ohio lost $2 billion in foregone revenue from its incentive in two years alone.

Jon Hamm and Wife Anna Osceola Have Welcomed Their First Baby—Inside the ‘Mad Men’ Star’s Bachelor Pad Turned Family Home

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (970 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Realtor

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, jon Hamm and Anna Osceola are officially parents!
  • The new bundle of joy is a boy, according to a People magazine source.
  • The couple, who met on the set of "Mad Men," first sparked speculation that they were expecting after Osceola, 38, was seen with a baby bump during a trip to the Hamptons—with sources swiftly confirming to People magazine that Hamm, 55, and his spouse were happily preparing to welcome a child.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, jon Hamm and Anna Osceola are officially parents! The "Your Friends & Neighbors" co-stars welcomed their first child together.

The new bundle of joy is a boy, according to a People magazine source.

The couple, who met on the set of "Mad Men," first sparked speculation that they were expecting after Osceola, 38, was seen with a baby bump during a trip to the Hamptons—with sources swiftly confirming to People magazine that Hamm, 55, and his spouse were happily preparing to welcome a child.

The actor—who tied the knot to Osceola in an intimate cliffside ceremony in California in 2023—broke his silence on those rumors during an appearance on “Late Night With Seth Meyers," telling Meyers that he was "very excited and deeply terrified" about becoming a dad.

“I think I’m doing it right," he stated, adding that those feelings shouldn't ever “go away.”.

He then poked fun at his age, teasing, "When your kid is 70, you’ll be like, ‘I did it!’ When I’m 152.”.

Back when rumors began surfacing that the couple was expecting, an unnamed insider told People, “Jon’s incredibly excited. This is something he and Anna have wanted and hoped for. He’s not thinking about his age or what anyone else has to say about it. He’s just really happy.”.

The source added that Hamm is "happy, settled, and ready" for the next stage of his life, while a different insider told Us Weekly that the couple was "trying to relax a bit but are enjoying making prepares for the baby.".

While the process of nesting can look entirely different from one family to the next, the news about Hamm and Osceola's upcoming addition does raise a question about whether the couple will raise the baby in the actor's longtime $4 million Los Feliz pad, which he purchased in 2017, before he was officially linked with his now-wife.

Though the home served as a bachelor pad for Hamm for several years, it has since become a marital residence for the couple and could now evolve once again—this time, into a family dwelling.

Certainly the four-bedroom, 3,600-square-foot home boasts plenty of room for a family of three. There's a spacious kitchen equipped with top-of-the-line appliances and a spacious pantry.

The 4.5 bathrooms feature spa-worthy furnishings, while the comfortable family room opens up to a stunning backyard patio complete with a built-in grill station, fire pit, and saltwater pool.

The property’s midcentury aesthetic makes it the kind of place one might picture the actor’s most notable on-screen character, Don Draper, residing, with wood paneling and asymmetrical design choices that ooze character while maintaining a peaceful environment.

The gated property is located at the end of a charming cul-de-sac in the Los Angeles neighborhood, which many substantial names in Hollywood have called home over the years, including Brad Pitt, Kristen Wiig, and Aubrey Plaza.

In a recent development, it’s not the first time Hamm has invested in the area, purchasing a 3,100-square-foot Los Feliz abode for $900,000 in 2002 with his then-partner, actress Jennifer Westfeldt. The duo parted ways in 2015 after spending 18 years together.

During his previous relationship, Hamm was not sold on the concept of fatherhood.

“I see my friends who have children and I’m like, ‘Dude, how are you even upright, much less here at work at 6 a.m.?” he candidly mentioned to Us in 2012.

However, he’s changed his tune since beginning a life with Osceola and is now “over the moon” at the thought of enjoying a fresh life as a dad, according to an Us Weekly source.

“Jon has always wanted to be a dad with Anna,” the source continued. “Having a family was something that was really important to both of them from the beginning.

"They’ve talked about this chapter for a long time and were always on the same page about wanting children, so for it to be actually happening now feels incredibly special.”.

The Emmy-winning performer has opened up about his desire to have a family with his wife, telling The Hollywood Reporter that, due to his parents’ divorce during his childhood, he “didn’t look at marriage as a thing,” but was hopeful for his own union to turn into a growing family.

Sources indicate that “I will be the old dad, but so it goes,” he remarked in 2024, then 53 years old. “It could be a good thing. We’ll see.”.

Hamm and Osceola first crossed paths in 2015, when filming the finale episode of “Mad Men” in Big Sur, CA.

Romance rumors swirled in 2017, but their relationship was not officially confirmed until 2020. The couple made their public red carpet debut at the Vanity Fair Oscars Party in 2022.

Hamm eventually popped the question. “I just knew at a certain point I wanted to be with this person,” he shared with The Hollywood Reporter in 2023. “But when I proposed, I was terrified. I was like, ‘What am I doing?’”.

The couple tied the knot in July 2023, with their sentimental wedding celebration serving as a thoughtful nod to their “Mad Men” roots.

The ceremony was held at Anderson Canyon, the Big Sur spot where they first met when filming the show’s final episode. Surrounded by loved ones and lush florals, they exchanged vows alongside the Pacific Ocean.

Industry News: AI inference servers shrink to fit the air-cooled racks enterprises already run

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Power-efficient inference chips are becoming the entry price for enterprises that want to run AI on hardware they own.
  • It has been revealed that as AI shifts from building models to running them every day, costly graphics processing unit racks and the liquid cooling they demand keep many companies renting compute instead.
  • It has been revealed that “Enterprises cannot own their own infrastructure.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UPDATED 14:29 EST / NOVEMBER 19 2026.

Power-efficient inference chips are becoming the entry price for enterprises that want to run AI on hardware they own.

It has been revealed that as AI shifts from building models to running them every day, costly graphics processing unit racks and the liquid cooling they demand keep many companies renting compute instead. That gap is opening room for challengers to the incumbent chipmakers. Axelera AI B.V. built its business at the edge with low-power chips and edge AI development tools, and it is now taking that technology into data center infrastructure, according to Manuel Botija (pictured), vice president and head of product at Axelera.

It has been revealed that “Enterprises cannot own their own infrastructure. They’re locked out because of the cost and the power,” Botija noted. “We are enabling them now to own it. It’s not that we are helping the world save power or save money — which we are — but it’s that we are unlocking use cases that were simply not possible before.”.

According to recent reports, botija spoke with theCUBE Research’s John Furrier and Rebecca Knight at SC26, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed how power-efficient inference chips are heading for the data center and how enterprises locked out by the cost and power of GPU racks can own their own AI infrastructure instead of renting compute. (* Disclosure below.).

“Having a six-kilowatt server that can perform like a data centre GPU is a pretty major deal,” he stated. “It basically means that they have some storage equipment, some networking equipment, some traditional CPU equipment, and next to all of that, they can also insert some AI inference hardware acceleration without needing to go and rebuild another server room or another data center.”.

Recent findings suggest that for enterprises that would rather own their AI hardware than pay a recurring cloud bill, the barriers have been steep. A GPU rack costs at least $1 million, often far more, and usually requires liquid cooling, Botija noted. Axelera’s answer rests on digital in-memory computing, a technique that grew out of its founders’ research and gives the firm’s power-efficient inference chips a performance-per-watt advantage.

“Now you can own your own infrastructure,” Botija said. “You can amortize those investments and … reduce your opex, and therefore be more profitable as a company.”.

Mortgage Calculator: Here’s How Much You Need To Buy a $430K Home at a 7.28% Rate

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (566 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Realtor

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Mortgage rates surged higher this week, reversing four consecutive weeks of declines as persistent inflation and geopolitical worries pushed borrowing costs back up.
  • The average rate on 30-year fixed home loans jumped to 7.28% for the week ending Nov.
  • Borrowing costs also remain substantially above where they stood a year ago, when rates averaged 6.26% during the same period in 2025.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Mortgage rates surged higher this week, reversing four consecutive weeks of declines as persistent inflation and geopolitical worries pushed borrowing costs back up.

The average rate on 30-year fixed home loans jumped to 7.28% for the week ending Nov. 19, up 17 basis points from 7.11% recorded the week before, according to Freddie Mac.

Borrowing costs also remain substantially above where they stood a year ago, when rates averaged 6.26% during the same period in 2025.

In a recent development, so what does this mean for homebuyers? Using the Realtor.com® mortgage calculator, we can look at how the math works out for the median-priced home in the U.S.

All examples assume a 30-year fixed mortgage and include principal and interest only, excluding property taxes, homeowners insurance, and mortgage insurance.

For a homebuyer eyeing the median house price of $430,000, a 20% down payment results in a loan amount of $344,000.

Sources indicate that at today's 7.28% rate, the monthly principal and interest payment is approximately $2,354. This reflects a $40 monthly increase from the previous week’s payment of $2,314.

Compared to the 6.26% average from November 2025, which required a $2,120 monthly payment for a home at this price, today’s buyers are paying $234 more every single month.

The monthly costs have also risen markedly for those using FHA loans with a 3.5% down payment.

On a $430,000 home, an FHA borrower would finance roughly $414,950. At today’s 7.28% rate, the monthly principal and interest payment comes to approximately $2,839.

This reflects a $48 increase from last week's monthly cost of $2,791. Compared to the 6.26% rates of November 2025, where the monthly payment for this loan amount sat at $2,558, today’s FHA borrowers are paying an extra $281 in interest every month.

However, looking back at the October 2023 peak of 7.79%, where the payment for a home at this price reached $2,984, today's monthly payment still offers $145 in relief.

The long-term financial picture shows how this abrupt reversal impacts total borrowing costs over a 30-year term.

A buyer with a 20% down payment at today’s 7.28% rate will pay a total of $847,328 in principal and interest over the life of the mortgage.

While this week's jump erased much of the ground gained over the past month, this total still represents a contrast to the October 2023 peak of 7.79%, when the total cost for that same $344,000 loan would have reached $890,630.

By securing a mortgage at today’s rate instead of that peak, a homebuyer effectively avoids $43,302 in interest charges over the 30-year loan life.

FHA borrowers see a similar trajectory of long-term figures. Financing the current median-priced home at today's 7.28% rate results in a lifetime payment of $1,022,090 for principal and interest.

If that same loan had been locked in at the 7.79% peak in late 2023, the total cost would have climbed to $1,074,323. This represents a total long-term savings of $52,233 for FHA buyers.

What we learned from Nvidia’s first earnings call without Jensen Huang

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 15 min read (2924 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Siliconangle

⏱️ ~15 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that nvidia Corp.
  • It has been revealed that revenue more than doubled year-over-year.
  • This was Nvidia’s first earnings call without co-founder Jensen Huang, whose resignation as president and chief executive was declared on Nov.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UPDATED 14:32 EST / NOVEMBER 19 2026.

ANALYSIS by Zeus Kerravala.

Recent findings suggest that nvidia Corp. reported its quarterly results this week, and contrary to the prevailing narrative, the sky didn’t fall.

It has been revealed that revenue more than doubled year-over-year. The Vera Rubin chip platform achieved the fastest product ramp in the firm’s history, and management raised its fiscal 2028 growth outlook to roughly 75%, up from 70%. By all accounts, it was a solid beat and raise.

This was Nvidia’s first earnings call without co-founder Jensen Huang, whose resignation as president and chief executive was declared on Nov. 12. Board Chair Harvey Jones told investors that the resignation followed the “disclosure of personal behavior inconsistent with the company’s code of conduct, standards, and cultural norms.” Hours after Huang publicly said he would be willing to return, Jones said the board “does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO” and would not take questions about the circumstances or the board’s ongoing investigation.

Colette Kress, the longtime chief financial officer who is now also serving as interim CEO, set the tone in her first minute: “Our ambition will not change. Our passion for innovation will not change, and our commitment to customers, partners, and shareholders will not change.”.

It has been revealed that after listening to the call, I believe Nvidia answered the short-term question and left the long-term one open. The organization made a convincing case that it can execute without its founder. It has yet to show who decides where it goes next. Here are five things we learned and what they mean for those who buy, budget for or operate artificial intelligence infrastructure.

It has been revealed that the fear going into the call was disruption. The quarter closed before Huang’s exit, so the results can’t settle that. The guidance can, and it went up. Hyperscalers brought Vera Rubin into production in about a month, half the time Grace Blackwell required. The roadmap is set through Vera Rubin Ultra next year and Feynman in 2028, and Kress stated the supply agreements extend through the end of the decade.

She explained that the past month has been “Business as usual.” Kress added, “We’ve engaged with our customers, suppliers and partners. They’re all 100% behind us.” She also noted that TSMC leadership was at Nvidia’s offices this week.

In a recent development, I have long held that Nvidia’s moat was never the silicon. It’s the accumulated layers of systems, software and supply chain built around it. The past week was the first real test of that view, and so far, it’s holding. A yearly product cadence this complex runs on thousands of engineers and a supply chain planned years in advance.

It has been revealed that asked about talent retention, Kress acknowledged that “there are diverse opinions” among employees while insisting they are “committed to doing their life’s work” at Nvidia. The tech giant’s talent can’t be overstated, and although Huang was the face of the company, the employees are what made it tick.

Earlier this week, Cisco Systems Inc. CEO Chuck Robbins appeared with Brian Sozzi. When asked whether he still trusts Nvidia, Robbins replied immediately, “Absolutely.” He added, “The industry’s bigger than one person. I don’t care how good you are. There are a lot of smart people. There are 42,000 people at Nvidia. So I’m not all that concerned.” Huang may have been the most visible Nvidia employee, but the firm is full of smart, driven people. Leadership understands this, and I expect turnover to have minimal impact.

Recent findings suggest that employee retention is a top-of-mind issue for Nvidia executives. Business Insider reported this week that the tech giant held its first all-hands meeting after Huang. The article noted that Kress unveiled plans to accelerate pay raises and equity grants, Jones discussed the CEO search and Buck outlined the roadmap. It’s reasonable to believe that Huang’s departure was a shock to employees, but the business goes on, and I expect things to settle down in short order.

For information technology buyers, nothing changes about what you’ve ordered or planned over the next 18 to 24 months. Don’t pause a deployment because of a leadership headline. The advice I gave in August still applies: Welcome Nvidia’s simplification and hedge the dependency.

Recent findings suggest that one of the more interesting comments on the call came from Jones, not Kress. In describing the CEO search, which will consider both internal and external candidates, he mentioned the board “appreciates that we’re living in a world where advanced silicon technologies and national security dynamics are driving major changes in our marketplace. Our newly introduced CEO will need to navigate those waters carefully.”.

That was paired with immediate action. On the morning of earnings, the board created a standing national security and export control oversight committee of three directors that will retain outside experts. Kress disclosed that Nvidia is no longer shipping licensed Hopper data center products to China and noted that the U.S. Commerce Department issued latest export controls this week, which the manufacturer “still has some time to study.”.

In a recent development, huang was a product visionary who also served as the industry’s chief diplomat. The board is now signaling that fluency in Washington is a core requirement, on par with technical vision.

For IT leaders at multinationals, export policy is now a deployment variable. The newly introduced Commerce rule is intended to block remote access to advanced chips via data centers in third countries, so the location of your capacity and who can access it are now compliance questions. Bring your compliance team into AI infrastructure planning early.

Industry observers note that with demand still far ahead of supply, who gets Nvidia systems matters more than what they cost. Kress laid out the criteria more clearly than I’ve heard before. First are land, power and shell, meaning whether a customer’s facility is ready to receive and use the gear in the quarter it ships. Second is capital. Third, for customers that aren’t investment-grade, is proof of off-take, or evidence that someone has committed to use the capacity.

“All are getting the same pricing,” Kress remarked. “That is super important for us, and we just need to assure that they are ready on their side in terms of being able to accept the compute.”.

Recent findings suggest that those same factors were incorporated into the guidance. Kress mentioned the outlook “considers data center readiness, the strength and durability of end customer demand, and our customers’ access to capital.” The reality is that the AI bottleneck has shifted from the chip to the building, the grid and the balance sheet. Nvidia is serving as the industry’s underwriter, determining who is ready.

Recent findings suggest that the lesson for enterprise buyers is that readiness is the currency. If you want on-premises systems, secure power, cooling and funding before requesting allocation. If you can’t, buy capacity from a provider that has already cleared this hurdle. In my view, this also helps explain why sovereign AI is growing so quickly for Nvidia. Those projects often arrive with land and power already in place.

Over the past year, Nvidia has used its balance sheet to seed the ecosystem through guarantees, investments, and commitments to neoclouds and AI labs. Though  neoclouds remain key, Kress brought a different tone to this audience. She said Nvidia will “continue to be disciplined and selective” in supporting neoclouds and that it is “rigorously evaluating future investments, commitments, and guarantees” as other sources of capital become available. Asked about vendor financing, she acknowledged that “a lot of things have changed over this last quarter.”.

According to recent reports, two notable details emerged during the call. When Bernstein Research analyst Stacy Rasgon pressed on what he read as new disclosure language about neocloud commitments, Kress explained that Nvidia’s guarantees take effect only after a partner has raised its own debt and equity, built the facility and installed the compute. If the project stalls, the guarantee lapses.

“Is it latest? No. Did we change anything? No,” she stated. Even so, spelling it out clarifies Nvidia’s participation in neoclouds. When asked about uses of capital beyond the share buyback, which she said Nvidia still aims to complete, she put suppliers first: “The top priority is going to be our suppliers.” Prepayments to expand capacity come before customer financing, which will be reserved for “very strong customers.”.

Sources indicate that this was a critical piece of information for investors. I’ve previously compared vendor-financed neoclouds to the CLECs of the internet era, where the financing organization was left holding the bag. A CFO-led Nvidia appears to see the same risk. The result is a shakeout in which well-capitalized neoclouds with contracted demand grow stronger, while thinly funded ones struggle to secure systems. This should offer some comfort to investors that circular financing has been de-risked.

The flip side is that someone still must fund the buildout outside the hyperscalers. Kress pointed to infrastructure capital partners establishing financing platforms. Whether that money arrives as fast as Nvidia steps back is what to watch for.

It has been revealed that my advice to IT buyers is to ask, before signing a multiyear deal with a neocloud, how it’s financed, how much capacity is committed and where it stands in Nvidia’s allocation queue. Those were niche questions a year ago. They should be standard due diligence now.

Sources indicate that the demand story has shifted from training models to running agents, broadening what customers need from Nvidia. Citing OpenRouter data, Kress noted agentic workloads now account for roughly 80% of tokens. Falling token prices are driving more usage, keeping GPU rental rates climbing.

In a recent development, the CPU growth story shouldn’t surprise anyone. In May, I wrote that agentic AI opens a massive new spigot for Nvidia on the CPU side. This quarter, demand outpaced supply. “Agentic AI is driving extraordinary demand for CPUs, far outstripping supply,” Kress stated, noting that Nvidia’s Vera CPU is now adopted by CoreWeave, Meta, Nscale and Open AI. Agents spend much of their time calling tools, running code and moving data, which is general-purpose work. A CPU shortage amid a GPU boom highlights how quickly the workload is changing.

Nvidia is also filling in the layers above and around the hardware. The agent safety platform pairs OpenShell, which limits what agents can access, with Sentry, which runs on BlueField data processing units and monitors agent behavior in silicon. In my view, the biggest barrier to deploying agents in production is control, not model quality.

It has been revealed that the network is part of this, too. Kress said co-packaged optics is in volume production, and Lambda’s deployment, announced at this week’s SC26 conference, is the first large-scale proof point. Nvidia is a formidable networking vendor, though buyers mixing accelerators will still want to weigh a network supplier that isn’t also selling a competing chip.

For IT buyers, strategy CPU capacity for agent workloads now, and insist that agent controls reside outside the model, in infrastructure you can audit.

The question of who the new CEO will be might not be just about Nvidia but about the entire industry. If the board goes internal, Ian Buck seems to be the frontrunner. Externally, the names most bandied about are Advanced Micro Devices Inc. CEO Lisa Su, Arm Ltd. CEO Rene Haas and Google Cloud CEO Thomas Kurian, or we could see Manuvir Das make a comeback and return to the tech giant.

Most industry watchers describe Nvidia as a chip manufacturer, a view that is about a decade out of date. Nvidia’s value comes from the full systems it has built around its silicon. Each is a stack tailored to an industry: hardware, libraries, frameworks, pretrained models, simulation and developer tools, all tuned to work together.

It has been revealed that the next CEO must treat silicon as a key layer of an open, secure, agentic enterprise stack. Enterprises won’t buy GPUs. They’ll buy outcomes: agents that run safely on governed data across clouds, on-premises and at the edge. Whoever runs Nvidia next must sell that outcome, play well within an ecosystem Nvidia doesn’t fully control, and make security a core part of the platform. Here are three dark-horse candidates to consider:.

In a recent development, matt Garman. The Amazon Web Services Inc. CEO has led the world’s largest cloud through the shift to AI. He knows what it takes to turn infrastructure into consumable services at enormous scale. Garman also lives the open-stack approach: AWS offers model choice, runs its own Trainium chips alongside Nvidia’s, and sells to enterprises that want flexibility rather than lock-in. He would bring operational discipline and a deep feel for the customer. The question is whether Nvidia’s biggest customer-turned-competitor can credibly lead the supplier.

Jeetu Patel, Cisco Systems Inc.’s president and chief product officer, is the best storyteller in enterprise tech after Huang himself. He has spent the past few years rebuilding Cisco’s portfolio around secure AI infrastructure, integrating networking, security and observability into a single platform. That is exactly the “open, secure, agentic” stack Nvidia must deliver. Patel thinks in platforms, moves swiftly,and has been personally using AI agents to shape his product views. He also has deep enterprise credibility, which Nvidia needs more than additional credibility with hyperscalers.

Charlie Giancarlo, CEO of Everpure (formerly Pure Storage), may be the most underrated name here. He built networking businesses at Cisco, spent time in private equity, and has repositioned Pure as a data management organization. Storage revenue is growing thanks to hyperscaler wins. Giancarlo understands that agentic AI depends on data and that the data layer and the network are where enterprise AI succeeds or fails. He is a systems thinker who has led a platform transition before.

Two final points on the CEO hire: For some reason, there is a tremendous amount of industry chatter that Jensen Huang was the only person at Nvidia with key relationships with suppliers, partners, and other ecosystem providers. I know for a fact that is not true. Nvidia’s leadership, which includes Buck, Deb Shoquist (executive vice president of operations), Nico Caprez (vice president of global AI development), Gilad Shainer and Kevin Deierling (networking leadership), Kress and others, all have deep relationships with the ecosystem.

Industry observers note that also, I wouldn’t expect the board to make a snap decision about its next CEO. The roadmap is baked beyond Feynman, and the firm can continue for a couple of years, if needed. This is an vital hire; the board should take its time and ensure it’s the right person.

This call confirmed what many industry watchers, including me, have long believed: The moat was built in layers, and those layers held. Supply is constrained, the roadmap is set and customers are still asking for more than Nvidia can build.

Kress closed the call by saying, “We’ve got this.” On execution, I believe her. Kress is a steady hand right now, and the discipline she brings to capital allocation should make the AI buildout healthier. The bets that created Nvidia’s position, though, were placed years before the market arrived. Post-Jensen, Nvidia will continue to perform as it did; as Robbins put it, no one is bigger than the industry.

My advice to IT buyers is to stick with current prepares and closely monitor the CEO search. Since Nvidia’s roadmap is baked through Feynman and beyond, it can ride momentum for the next two years or longer.

Zeus Kerravala is a principal analyst at ZK Research, a division of Kerravala Consulting. He wrote this article for SiliconANGLE.

The Houses That Made Newly introduced Orleans—and the Rising Cost of Keeping Them Standing

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1589 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Realtor

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The World Monuments Fund's 2026 Irreplaceable America list recognizes the kind of architecture that has come to define the country—landmarks that serve as reminders of who we are and where we came from.
  • But one place was so emblematic of the country's past, present, and future that no single building could serve as a symbol of the whole.
  • Fresh Orleans is the only entire city among the 10 places to receive the designation.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The World Monuments Fund's 2026 Irreplaceable America list recognizes the kind of architecture that has come to define the country—landmarks that serve as reminders of who we are and where we came from.

But one place was so emblematic of the country's past, present, and future that no single building could serve as a symbol of the whole.

Fresh Orleans is the only entire city among the 10 places to receive the designation.

“New Orleans itself is irreplaceable—not just one building, one district or one monument, but the entire living city,” says Kristin Gisleson Palmer, executive director of the Preservation Resource Center of New Orleans when the title was unveiled.

Yet the buildings that earned the city that recognition now face a mounting threat: the cost of protecting them.

Latest Orleans has the second-highest homeowners insurance costs relative to property values among the nation's 100 largest metro areas, according to research from Realtor.com®. Now, as storms intensify and insurance costs rise, the city's historic homes are becoming more expensive to protect and preserve.

On a recent walking tour through Bayou St. John, Heather Veneziano—director of Tulane University's Historic Preservation Program, who helped spearhead the city's nomination—began not with a building, but with the ground beneath our feet.

Industry observers note that the bayou that gives the neighborhood its name connects to Lake Pontchartrain, a brackish estuary fed by rivers and linked to the Gulf of Mexico. The slower-moving waters served Indigenous communities as a transportation route before European colonization.

Alongside that access, nearby natural ridges offered comparatively high ground in a landscape shaped by water, making the area an appealing, if imperfect, place to settle.

Sources indicate that but higher ground didn't always mean dry ground. And the European settlers who followed knew the water would eventually return, and they built their homes accordingly.

“You have to build for place,” Veneziano tells Realtor.com.

It has been revealed that at the Pitot House, a Creole colonial country house built in 1799, she pointed to the elevated living quarters as an example. The ground level, she said, could be used for storage during dry seasons, while allowing floodwater to enter below the principal rooms during wet ones.

“You lived, I think, with the knowledge that water is going to be a thing you can't fight against,” Veneziano noted.

Industry observers note that that understanding shaped the building from the ground up. Its broad roof and galleries offered shelter from the elements, while its timber framing incorporated cypress, a locally abundant wood prized for its resistance to decay and insects.

Residents adapted that approach across generations, raising homes as newly introduced neighborhoods and architectural forms developed, according to FEMA's history of building elevation in New Orleans.

But even the most carefully adapted homes can't eliminate the danger.

Today, an estimated 88.9% of residential property value in the Fresh Orleans–Metairie metro faces severe or extreme flood risk, according to the 2025 Housing and Climate Risk Report from Realtor.com.

As Fresh Orleans grew, new residents brought their own architectural traditions, transforming both the appearance of its neighborhoods and the ways people lived within them.

The Creole townhouse, with shops beneath upper-floor residences and courtyards tucked behind masonry facades, became a defining feature of the French Quarter.

Recent findings suggest that interestingly, its appearance was partly shaped by disaster. After fires destroyed much of the city in 1788 and 1794, Spanish authorities favored more fire-resistant construction, helping establish the brick, stucco, and ironwork associated with the neighborhood today.

Newly introduced Orleans' celebrated architecture was also built on slavery.

Industry observers note that behind the ornate facades, enslaved people lived in courtyard quarters and worked in the homes they helped construct. Enslaved craftspeople helped construct the homes themselves, while the city's wealth was deeply tied to their forced labor.

Yet within this slaveholding society, free Black Upcoming Orleanians also established themselves as builders and property owners. Architectural historian Tara A. Dudley has documented how the Dolliole and Soulié families shaped the city's housing and built wealth through real estate, despite laws restricting Black economic independence.

Following the Louisiana Purchase in 1803, Anglo-American settlers introduced different architectural preferences. Wealthy merchants built double-gallery houses Uptown, their stacked porches and classical columns reflecting fortunes tied to shipping, cotton, and enslaved peoples.

The craftsmanship that distinguished these homes also presents a modern financial challenge.

Rami Sneineh, a licensed insurance producer and owner of Insurance Navy Brokers, indicates replacing handmade windows, woodwork, or plaster may require scarce materials and specialized craftspeople.

“If your home sustained significant damage, it could take months to source similar materials and you’d likely need to hire specialized craftsmen to restore those one-of-a-kind details,” he says.

An older home worth $400,000, he offers as a hypothetical example, might cost $700,000 to reconstruct with comparable details.

But not every architectural tradition emerged from wealth.

The shotgun house, which spread through working-class neighborhoods during the 19th century, arranged narrow rooms one behind another. Its origins are debated, but historians have identified possible African and Caribbean influences. Double shotguns accommodated two households beneath one roof, making efficient use of narrow lots.

According to recent reports, and as drainage technology opened lower-lying areas to development, raised-basement houses appeared in neighborhoods such as Broadmoor and Mid-City. Their main living quarters sat a full story above the ground, carrying the tradition of elevation into the 20th century.

Yet the pumping systems that enabled the city's expansion also contributed to land subsidence, according to the Historic New Orleans Collection.

The homes remained elevated, but their protection increasingly depended on an engineered system of drainage, pumps, and levees—whose vulnerabilities became devastatingly apparent during Hurricane Katrina.

In a recent development, as we walked through Bayou St. John, the distant sound of a marching band practicing for upcoming Mardi Gras parades drifted across the neighborhood. Veneziano paused to listen, reflecting on the communities hidden behind and whithin the structures that surrounded us.

In a recent development, “The architecture is the setting for those relationships,” she said. “And people's voices are told through the built environment in which they live.”.

Today, Upcoming Orleans has 26 historic districts listed on the National Register of Historic Places, covering more than 45,000 properties and roughly 40% of its urbanized area.

But preserving the appearance of those neighborhoods doesn't always preserve the communities within them.

During our walk, Veneziano pointed out double shotguns converted into single-family homes, a trend she said accelerated after Hurricane Katrina. The exteriors might remain recognizable even as two residences become one.

“It's taking away affordable housing for the rental population because there's not as many rental units anymore,” she mentioned.

The lost rental unit also means losing a potential source of income that could help an owner maintain an aging structure.

And for the homeowners who do remain, those costs are rising on many fronts.

Single-family homes in the area carry an estimated annual homeowners insurance premium of $8,328, according to research from Realtor.com—equivalent to 3.6% of its median market value, and the second-highest burden among the 100 largest metropolitan areas.

Those estimates don't even account for the specialized demands of restoring historic architecture or purchasing separate flood coverage.

Even insured owners can face substantial out of pocket expenses. Sneineh notes that a 5% hurricane deductible on a home insured for $600,000 leaves an owner responsible for $30,000 before the insurer covers eligible damage.

“Properties that were previously affordable to purchase may now be unaffordable to insure,” claims Mujahid Merchant, an independent researcher in climate risk and mortgage credit.

When private coverage becomes unavailable, homeowners may turn to Louisiana Citizens, the state's insurer of last resort, which is required to charge higher rates than qualifying private insurers.

Sources indicate that and if a mortgaged home loses required coverage, its lender may purchase more expensive insurance and charge the owner. Merchant warns that the resulting increase in monthly payments can contribute to delinquency or foreclosure.

Yet some of the solutions draw on the same practical ingenuity that shaped these homes in the first place.

“Contrary to popular belief, you can strengthen your historic home’s roof without changing its historic look,” Sneineh says.

Recent findings suggest that louisiana's Fortify Homes Program offers eligible owners grants of up to $10,000 to strengthen roofs against hurricane winds. A state report found that median recipients saved $1,250 a year, or 22%, on insurance premiums. Upcoming Orleans also provides an expedited review process for qualifying roof replacements in local historic districts.

But even as owners find new ways to protect their homes from the elements, keeping those buildings affordable presents a different challenge.

Sources indicate that after Hurricane Katrina, thousands of Upcoming Orleanians left for cities such as Houston and Atlanta. Not everyone returned.

Veneziano described the familiarity of living near former teachers, relatives, and neighbors whose lives have intertwined for generations—connections that can't simply be reconstructed in another place.

“You can't take what you have anywhere and put it somewhere else,” she said. “Places don't matter without people.".

#18994. Enterprise AI is pushing cloud infrastructure beyond the GPU

Enterprise AI is pushing cloud infrastructure beyond the GPU

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1997 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Siliconangle

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that enterprise adoption of artificial intelligence is creating upcoming requirements for enterprise AI infrastructure.
  • In a recent development, agentic AI systems need environments where they can execute code, access data, connect to enterprise applications and operate securely across distributed infrastructure.
  • That shift is creating an opportunity for neocloud providers, but it is also changing what enterprises expect from them.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UPDATED 16:07 EST / NOVEMBER 19 2026.

Industry observers note that enterprise adoption of artificial intelligence is creating upcoming requirements for enterprise AI infrastructure. While much of the early AI investment centered on access to powerful GPUs, organizations moving AI applications and agents into production are discovering that accelerators are only one part of the equation.

In a recent development, agentic AI systems need environments where they can execute code, access data, connect to enterprise applications and operate securely across distributed infrastructure. That requires more than bare-metal GPU capacity. It calls for a complete cloud platform that combines compute, networking, storage, security and the services needed to manage applications at scale.

That shift is creating an opportunity for neocloud providers, but it is also changing what enterprises expect from them. Infrastructure providers increasingly need to support the full application lifecycle rather than simply supply specialized hardware.

During a live interview at KubeCon + CloudNativeCon North America 2026, theCUBE Research’s Paul Nashawaty spoke with Kevin Cochrane, chief marketing officer at Vultr, about the changing requirements of enterprise AI infrastructure, the return of CPU-based computing, data sovereignty and the growing role of platform engineering.

According to recent reports, “They need a full cloud platform,” Cochrane mentioned. “They need cloud compute, specialized AI compute, networking, storage and an open ecosystem.”.

Vultr entered the cloud market in 2014 with a developer-focused platform built around performance, cost efficiency and accessibility. Since then, the organization has expanded into AI infrastructure, offering both traditional cloud services and specialized GPU resources.

Cochrane said Vultr took a deliberate approach to the AI infrastructure market, prioritizing enterprise workload and platform-engineering requirements rather than focusing exclusively on GPU availability.

“We’ve always said that we’re the tortoise in AI infrastructure,” he said.

That approach reflects a broader change in how enterprises are approaching AI. Early infrastructure demand largely came from hyperscalers, AI research organizations and startups building large-scale models. Those customers needed access to GPU clusters, often through bare-metal infrastructure.

The next phase is different. Enterprises are looking to use AI agents to streamline operations, improve customer experiences and create latest revenue opportunities. Those applications must work alongside existing enterprise systems, comply with security requirements and integrate with established network and application architectures.

Recent findings suggest that bare-metal GPU infrastructure alone does not address those needs. Cochrane identified complexity and a lack of specialized skills as major obstacles to enterprise AI adoption. Organizations may have access to powerful accelerators, but they still need the surrounding infrastructure and services to build, deploy and operate applications.

Vultr’s strategy is to provide a more integrated environment, including traditional cloud compute, GPU infrastructure, networking, storage and access to cloud-native projects. Cochrane remarked the platform supports more than 60 Cloud Native Computing Foundation projects that customers can deploy directly.

The goal is to reduce the work required to assemble an AI environment. Rather than making enterprises integrate every component themselves, providers can offer preconfigured services and composable infrastructure that developers can deploy as needed.

That distinction is becoming important as AI moves beyond experimentation. Enterprises need infrastructure that supports production applications, not just model training and inference.

The growing focus on GPUs has sometimes obscured the role of traditional computing resources in AI architectures. But agentic AI is expanding the range of workloads that infrastructure providers must support.

According to recent reports, an AI agent does more than send a prompt to a model and receive a response. It may execute scripts, interact with repositories, run builds, access databases and invoke external tools. Those activities require compute resources beyond the GPU.

“Not all workloads need to be on a GPU,” Cochrane noted.

Industry observers note that CPUs remain essential for databases, application code and data pipelines. They can also support smaller, optimized open-source models and inference workloads that do not require dedicated accelerators.

Another emerging requirement is the environment in which agents execute tasks. As agents gain the ability to run code and interact with systems, enterprises need secure sandboxes that isolate those activities from production environments and sensitive resources.

Cochrane pointed to work underway in the cloud-native ecosystem around safe and secure agent sandboxes as an indication of how infrastructure requirements are changing.

This creates a more complex infrastructure model. GPUs may handle demanding model reasoning and inference, while CPUs support the applications, pipelines and execution environments surrounding those models.

Industry observers note that for organizations, the implication is that enterprise AI infrastructure decisions should account for the entire agentic workflow. Buying GPU capacity without considering the compute, storage, networking and isolation requirements around it can create another infrastructure silo. A full-stack approach gives platform teams more flexibility to match resources to individual workloads while maintaining a consistent operational environment.

As enterprises expand AI deployments across regions, data sovereignty is becoming more than a question of where information is stored.

Organizations operating in regulated industries or under national data requirements need to understand where data resides, which services can access it and what happens if infrastructure outside a particular region becomes unavailable.

Sources indicate that cochrane described Vultr’s regional architecture as an isolation model in which each of its 34 global data center regions operates independently. According to him, data within a region remains resident there and is not accessed by Vultr services outside that region.

Sources indicate that the distinction extends beyond data residency to application operations. Cochrane used France as an example. An application running in a French region should continue operating even if Vultr’s global control plane and its other regions become unavailable.

In a recent development, “If the rest of the world went dark, your production application in France? It just runs,” he stated.

That approach is intended to reduce dependencies on global services that could otherwise affect regional application availability. It also gives organizations a clearer boundary for managing sensitive workloads and maintaining operational continuity.

For enterprises, this is an key architectural consideration. A cloud provider may offer regional data storage, but that does not necessarily mean every service required to operate an application is isolated within the same geography.

As AI applications become more deeply integrated into business operations, organizations will need to evaluate sovereignty across the full application stack, including data, compute, management services and operational dependencies.

The cost of running AI applications is becoming another major consideration as organizations move from pilots to sustained production workloads.

Inference costs can increase rapidly when agents repeatedly call models, retrieve information and execute multi-step workflows. As usage grows, enterprises must balance model performance, throughput and infrastructure expense.

In a recent development, cochrane believes some organizations will increasingly turn to open-source models that can be adapted to their own data and operated on infrastructure they control. Rather than relying entirely on large commercial models for every task, enterprises can post-train specialized models using proprietary information and deploy them for operational workloads where that approach makes sense.

It has been revealed that he described an example involving a platform engineering organization that reduced inference costs by 80% by post-training an open-source model and running it on its own infrastructure. The example illustrates a potential economic advantage, although results will depend on the workload, model, infrastructure and operational requirements involved.

According to recent reports, the broader point is that organizations are beginning to evaluate the economics of enterprise AI infrastructure across the entire stack. Model selection matters, but so do infrastructure utilization, throughput, data movement and the cost of operating agents over time.

For some workloads, owning more of the infrastructure and model lifecycle may provide better cost control than depending entirely on external inference services.

That does not mean every enterprise should build and operate its own models. It does suggest that organizations need more flexibility to choose where models run and how workloads are distributed.

The changing infrastructure requirements of agentic AI are also expanding the responsibilities of platform engineering teams.

Cochrane expects platform engineers to become central to enterprise AI adoption, working more closely with business units to understand which agents and preconfigured application environments are needed across the organization.

Sources indicate that that moves platform engineering beyond infrastructure provisioning and developer enablement. Teams will increasingly need to help define the building blocks that allow developers to deploy governed AI applications without having to assemble every component independently.

Cochrane also sees an opportunity for the cloud-native community to evolve how it shares infrastructure patterns. The CNCF ecosystem has helped developers adopt individual open-source projects across networking, storage, observability and other infrastructure categories. But as architectures become more complex, organizations need guidance on how those components fit together.

Industry observers note that cochrane predicted the emergence of marketplaces where developers can share opinionated, prebuilt stacks for specific workload types. Instead of selecting and configuring individual components, teams could start with a tested architecture and adapt it to their requirements. That could help reduce the complexity of building agentic applications while encouraging more consistent deployment practices.

Industry observers note that he also expects consolidation in the neocloud market. Providers focused primarily on bare-metal GPU capacity may face pressure as enterprises demand broader cloud capabilities. Those able to expand into full public cloud platforms could be better positioned to serve production workloads.

Vultr’s existing cloud platform gives it a foundation for that transition, Cochrane mentioned, with its investments in both traditional compute and specialized AI infrastructure.

Enterprise AI is changing the definition of cloud infrastructure. GPUs remain vital, but agentic applications require a broader foundation that includes CPUs, secure execution environments, networking, storage, data sovereignty and integrated cloud-native services.

That creates an opportunity for providers that can deliver more than specialized accelerator capacity. It also puts platform engineering teams in a more strategic position as enterprises work to standardize how AI applications are built, deployed and governed.

The next phase of the neocloud market may therefore be determined less by who can offer the most GPU capacity and more by who can provide the complete environment enterprises need to run AI in production.

As Cochrane’s comments suggest, the infrastructure challenge is no longer simply making AI compute available. It is making the entire system around AI practical to operate at enterprise scale.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Angelina Jolie is ushering in a new era after quitting Los Angeles.

In the wake of selling the $24.75 million California estate she snapped up less than a year after filing for divorce from Brad Pitt in 2017, the actress has revealed looks to enjoy more time overseas and less time tied down to a singular location.

Jolie recently visited Cambodia, where local outlets reported she met with religious leaders. The “Maleficent” star reportedly “paid her respects and presented religious offerings” to Samdech Preah Maha Sumeatheathibodi Am Limheng, supreme patriarch of the Mohanikay Buddhist order.

She also visited a traditional crafts village on Cambodia's Koh Dach, which is known as Silk Island, to observe local artisans.

The mom of six detailed her special connection to the country during earlier travels to the Philippines, where she spoke on a Nov. 11 panel alongside Cambodian filmmaker Rithy Panh.

It has been revealed that “I found this place and the people to be so warm and so open, and I couldn’t believe their spirits were so strong after all they have suffered,” Jolie said of Cambodia. “You go to certain places, and you just feel at home.”.

According to People magazine, the actress looks to expand her creative collective, Atelier Jolie, with a residency in Cambodia in 2017.

The effort will be a partnership between Panh’s Bophana Center and the Maddox Foundation, which Jolie founded in 2003 and named for her eldest child, Maddox Jolie, whom she adopted from Battambang, Cambodia, in 2002.

According to the Atelier Jolie website, the business is focused on “the discovery of art, craft and design work from cultures around the world.” She founded the certified B Corporation business in 2023, with a headquarters in Manhattan’s NoHo neighborhood, which serves as a retail store, art space, and cultural center.

Jolie spoke about her plans for the future in a September 2026 interview with L’Officiel, noting that she plans to spend more time “out of the States.”.

“The hope for the atelier was always to be global,” she stated. “The idea would be to visit the different locations around the world and meet local artists and makers.”.

She noted a desire to expand the atelier to Brazil, as well as “get back to doing more hands-on work” with the Maddox Foundation in Cambodia.

She also expressed a desire to live a life that’s less tied down to one specific locale.

It has been revealed that “I don’t really plan to have a base,” Jolie admitted. “I’d like to have a home base for my family, a place where some of the mom stuff and the family photos are. And then I’d like to be a bit nomadic for a while.”.

The star also noted that she has a home in Cambodia, which “will also be a residency a few months out of the year for the Khmer culture.”.

Jolie’s appreciation for the Southeast Asian country began when she first visited to film the 2001 movie “Lara Croft: Tomb Raider.” She returned a year later to adopt her son and has since spent lots of time traveling back and forth with her family.

In 2017, she directed “First They Killed My Father,” a Khmer-language biographical thriller based on a memoir of the same name by Cambodian human rights activist Loung Ung.

In a People magazine interview, Jolie revealed Maddox—who was 15 at the time—was deeply involved in the creation of the film and helped with research.

Jole revealed her son spent “over four months” in the country at that time, “really reading, listening, learning, and absorbing all things about his culture and his country, including the very, very dark parts.”.

Although Jolie was born and raised in Los Angeles, she has long expressed her desire to leave the city.

Recent findings suggest that “I grew up in this town. I am here because I have to be here from a divorce,” she told The Hollywood Reporter in 2024. She explained that once her youngest children—twins Knox Leon and Vivienne Marcheline—turned 18, she’d be “able to leave.”.

The milestone birthday passed this July, paving the way for a new chapter for Jolie.

“It’s the end of a certain time for me,” she told L’Officiel weeks later.

Jolie made moves quickly, putting her idyllic Los Angeles compound on the market for $29.9 million in May, seemingly in anticipation of Knox and Vivienne’s 18th.

The six-bedroom, 10-bathroom abode found a buyer in September, selling for $24.75 million. Jolie had originally purchased the home for $24.5 million in 2017, and it served as her primary residence for nearly a decade.

While Jolie plans to spend the bulk of her time jet-setting, she hasn’t said goodbye to the United States for good, and has reportedly purchased a Connecticut mansion, according to Page Six Hollywood.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that bitcoin’s latest price decline may be setting the stage for a familiar market pattern, and history could give bulls reason to be optimistic. The benchmark cryptocurrency has suffered a sharp drop ahead of Anthropic’s upcoming red-hot stock market debut, echoing its 19% plunge in the 50 days leading up to SpaceX’s IPO earlier this year. However, if the historical pattern repeats, Bitcoin could be gearing up for a significant recovery, with a potential rebound toward $90,000 by February now drawing attention.

Industry observers note that strive CEO Matt Cole has observed an interesting historical parallel between Bitcoin’s current price action and its performance ahead of SpaceX’s record-breaking IPO. In the 50 days leading up to SpaceX’s $75 billion public debut on June 12, Bitcoin plunged 19%.

Now, with Anthropic preparing for a potential $64.4 billion IPO next week, BTC has posted a remarkably similar 18% decline over the same period, Cole noted in a post on X.

At press time, Bitcoin was trading at $64,665, according to CoinGecko, extending its recent losses after breaking below the $70,000 mark on November 13. The cryptocurrency continued its downward slide over the weekend, falling beneath $67,000 as bearish pressure intensified.

The Strive chief noted that overlaying the two price movements reveals an almost identical pattern, raising the possibility that Bitcoin could be repeating its pre-SpaceX sell-off ahead of another historic market debut.

Bitcoin extended its decline after SpaceX’s market debut, reaching its lowest point 18 days later before reversing course. The subsequent rally lifted BTC 28% above its IPO-day closing price within 100 days.

“If Anthropic follows the same pattern, most of the drawdown is behind us, and it could reverse quickly over the next couple of months,” Cole opined.

If history repeats itself, Bitcoin could climb toward $90,000 by late February, Cole suggested.

Binance co-founder Changpeng “CZ” Zhao also weighed in on the chart comparison, sharing the analysis on X and describing Cole’s findings as “interesting.”.

It has been revealed that however, the historical comparison comes with key caveats. Dogecoin co-creator Billy Markus, who goes by Shibetoshi Nakamoto on X, has weighed in on Bitcoin's potential role as an alternative to traditional retirement savings, describing Bitcoin as having the "best reason to exist.".

A 401(k) is an employer-sponsored retirement savings proposal in the United States that typically allows workers to invest through a selection of financial products, often including mutual funds and exchange-traded funds.

In a recent development, the discussion began on X as market participants reacted to the ongoing market crash, which has seen millions of dollars in liquidations in the last 24 hours. Leveraged traders took the brunt, with $1.92 billion of liquidations over 24 hours, according to CoinGlass data. Longs accounted for the majority of the damage at $1.59 billion, while short liquidations totaled $341.26 million.

Bitcoin fell to a three-month low below $63,000; Dogecoin fell to a low of $0.055, last seen in June 2023. At the time of writing, Dogecoin was down 4.63% over the last 24 hours to $0.059.

An X user commented, apparently in light of the market drop, "Cash out or crash out.".

@mikethree bitcoin has the best reason to exist as the og, ethereum is a massive failure of its own goals but has positive brand recognition, they’re all dumb tokens for degenerates.

Dogecoin cofounder Billy Markus responded, saying, "I just sell immediately and hold very little since the market is just a delusion indicator and that’s too random to track.".

Another X user joined the discussion, saying Bitcoin remains "a good 401k replacement imo but depends on risk profile obviously." Markus replied to this, saying, "Bitcoin has the best reason to exist as the OG.".

As cryptocurrency adoption increases, more traditionally-minded investors have begun exploring digital assets as part of their retirement plans.

Asset manager Fidelity allows Bitcoin in 401(k) looks, depending on employer approval. Fidelity is primarily known for its huge portfolio of retirement accounts and is among the largest 401(k) providers in the U.S. Fidelity also has a standard account option, announced in April 2022, that allows employees with 401(k) accounts to add Bitcoin, in addition to its more traditional accounts.

Sources indicate that fidelity Investments confirmed a new retirement strategy in 2025 allowing U.S. adults to directly invest in cryptocurrencies such as Bitcoin, Ethereum and Litecoin.

Medical AI startup Boltz raises $110M to speed up small molecule research

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (851 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Siliconangle

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Boltz PBC, a startup that develops artificial intelligence models for pharmaceutical researchers, has raised $110 million in funding.
  • According to recent reports, bessemer led the Series A investment.
  • Small molecules, the building blocks of many drugs, can only neutralize a pathogen after binding to it.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UPDATED 16:17 EST / NOVEMBER 19 2026.

Boltz PBC, a startup that develops artificial intelligence models for pharmaceutical researchers, has raised $110 million in funding.

According to recent reports, bessemer led the Series A investment. Boltz stated on Wednesday that the fund was joined by a large group of new and returning backers. The consortium included Greycroft, Andreessen Horowitz, Amplify Partners, F-Prime Capital, Hummingbird and others.

Small molecules, the building blocks of many drugs, can only neutralize a pathogen after binding to it. As a result, researchers start drug discovery projects by looking for molecules that have a high binding affinity with pathogens. They often review hundreds of thousands of candidate molecules per project. The process can take months and often costs millions of dollars.

Boltz offers an AI model called BoltzMol-1 that speeds up the workflow. It generates binding affinity data by reviewing only a few dozen, particularly promising molecules instead of the hundreds of thousands usually needed. The fewer molecules need to be studied, the less time the analysis takes.

According to recent reports, binding affinity evaluations don’t yield drug discoveries right away. Instead, they produce data points called small molecule hits. Those are essentially faint clues that help researchers pinpoint the area where they should focus their efforts.

In a recent development, boltz staffers asked BoltzMol-1 to look for small molecule hits across 10 “challenging and therapeutically-relevant targets.” Targets are biological building blocks that play a role in disease processes. According to the firm, the model found small molecule hits for six of the targets.

Scientists can adapt BoltzMol-1 to project-specific constraints. If a research team has access to a relatively limited number of compounds, it could configure the model to only consider small molecules that can be made from those compounds. When material procurement is not an obstacle, BoltzMol-1 evaluates a much larger number of candidates.

Recent findings suggest that the manufacturer also offers a second model called BoltzProt-1. It can generate tens of thousands of protein designs based on data gleaned from small molecule hits. Additionally, BoltzProt-1 automatically reviews each protein to determine if it could be used to develop a fresh drug.

Usually, AI models evaluate protein designs based on rubrics that provide only an indirect view of their effectiveness. BoltzProt-1 uses more direct metrics. The tech giant states that BoltzProt-1’s protein evaluation mechanism demonstrated “higher success” than several competing models during internal tests.

Boltz sells its algorithms via an application programming interface that is billed based on token usage. According to the company, customers’ token consumption has grown by a factor of 50 since BoltzMol-1 and BoltzProt-1 launched in June. Boltz counts six of the world’s 20 largest pharmaceutical companies as clients.

In a recent development, the firm will use its fresh funding to grow its headcount and procure more computing infrastructure. The extra hardware should make it easier for Boltz to keep up with leading AI labs such as newly public Anthropic PBC and OpenAI Group. Over the past year, both companies have introduced models that are highly adapted to biology research tasks.

Boltz has already started training a upcoming generation of molecule design algorithms. The firm indicates that they are “showing substantial improvements” over its current models.

According to recent reports, chandler Fang, founder of AI payments startup t54.ai, has said that the organization's x402 Facilitator on the XRP Ledger (XRPL) has processed more than 10 million AI agent transactions. Fang made the comments in an interview that the XRPL Foundation published on X on November 15, and the interviewer put the number of these payments at 11.7 million.

Recent findings suggest that according to Fang, XRPL had almost no transactions made by AI agents three or four months before the interview, which was recorded at XRP Seoul 2026. "The entire volume got ramped up very quickly in the three months," he noted.

The x402 Facilitator works as a bridge between AI agents and payments, and agents can use XRP or the RLUSD stablecoin to move money without a separate wallet setup for every agent. Fang remarked that more than 200 merchants are already on the network.

According to Fang, the most common use case is paying for AI compute. Instead of paying $20 to $200 a month for an AI subscription, an agent can pay around $1 or 50 cents for a single task. "Instead, they can purchase this single compute for about $1, or 50 cents, and it can be settled on the XRPL," Fang stated.

Fang mentioned that such payments have low value and high frequency, so the high throughput and low fees of XRPL give the network an advantage. He also expects agent payments to move into real-life purchases over the next few quarters. "We have the coffee shop right outside our booth, right? And we are trying to empower users to use XRP and agent payments to finish a real-life transaction," Fang said.

According to Fang, trust is the main issue for agent payments, and t54.ai's Trustline product focuses on risk management for the financial activity of AI agents. He compared the service with the chargeback feature of credit cards. "So there is no lawsuit. It is a similar experience for agents," Fang said.

It has been revealed that t54.ai is also part of Mastercard's agentic payment program, where the startup is responsible for risk management. The x402 Facilitator processes transactions based on Mastercard Verifiable Intent, a protocol that verifies the behavior of AI agents.

Fang mentioned that t54.ai, Ripple and Mastercard are in talks about a three-way collaboration, and the first results will be shown at an upcoming hackathon.

It has been revealed that "The ten million transactions are just a starting point. I think next year you should expect a lot more transactions. Maybe even more transactions settled on XRPL will be done by AI agents than by humans," Fang remarked.
